items.prompt: What is complete metamorphosis, the pattern a butterfly's life follows?

options.label: Growing steadily larger without changing shape
options.feedback: That pattern belongs to insects like grasshoppers, which hatch looking like small adults and simply enlarge. A butterfly changes shape entirely between stages.

options.label: Shedding its skin twice and staying the same shape
options.feedback: Shedding skin does happen, but shape changes completely between stages rather than staying the same.

options.label: Passing through four separate body forms: egg, larva, pupa and adult
options.feedback: Each of the four stages looks and functions differently from the one before it.

options.label: Changing color as it ages but keeping the same body
options.feedback: A color change alone would leave the same crawling body throughout. A butterfly's body plan itself is rebuilt.

items.ko_title: More than a change of color
items.ko_line: Metamorphosis means the whole body plan changes, not just its size or shade.
items.exp_text: Complete metamorphosis means the egg, the larva, the pupa and the adult look and work nothing alike, unlike an insect that just grows bigger while keeping one body plan throughout. The caterpillar hatching from the egg is built only to eat and grow; inside the pupa that body is taken apart and rebuilt; the adult that finally emerges is built only to fly, feed and mate. Each stage hands off to the next once its own job is finished.

items.prompt: What actually happens to a caterpillar's body inside the chrysalis?

options.label: It falls still and only its outer color changes
options.feedback: The change reaches far deeper than color. Most of the internal tissue itself is broken down and rebuilt.

options.label: Most of its tissue breaks down and is rebuilt by cell clusters already present in its body
options.feedback: Enzymes dismantle the old tissue, and clusters of cells present since hatching use the material to build the adult.

options.label: It grows a new outer skin while every internal organ stays as it was
options.feedback: The change is not limited to the skin. Muscle and other internal tissue are broken down along with it.

options.label: It simply stops eating and shrinks until only wings are left
options.feedback: Shrinking from hunger would not explain where legs, antennae and eyes come from. Those parts are actively built, not left behind.

items.ok_line: Torn down and rebuilt from parts kept in reserve.
items.ko_line: The rebuilding happens throughout the body, not just on its outer covering.
items.exp_text: Enzymes released inside the pupa break down most of the caterpillar's muscle and other tissue into raw material. Scattered through its body since it hatched were small clusters of cells called imaginal discs, one set for each adult part — wings, legs, antennae, eyes. Fed by that broken-down material, each disc unfolds and grows into its adult structure, turning a crawling, chewing body into a flying, feeding one.

items.prompt: Why does a caterpillar shed its skin several times as it grows?

options.label: Its skin gets dirty and needs replacing
options.feedback: Dirt would wash or flake off on its own. What forces the shedding is the skin's own stiffness, not cleanliness.

options.label: Its outer covering cannot stretch, so a looser one must form underneath first
options.feedback: The firm outer cuticle stays a fixed size while the caterpillar keeps eating and growing beneath it.

options.label: It sheds skin to change color for camouflage
options.feedback: A caterpillar's color can shift between molts, but that is a side effect, not the reason for molting itself.

options.label: It loses skin naturally the way a person loses hair
options.feedback: Hair falls a few strands at a time without a size limit forcing it. A caterpillar sheds its whole covering at once, driven by growth.

items.ok_line: A rigid covering has to be replaced, not stretched.
items.ko_title: Think about the covering, not its color
items.ko_line: The trigger is a size limit built into the caterpillar's outer layer.
items.exp_title: A covering that will not stretch
items.exp_text: A caterpillar's outer layer is a firm cuticle rather than stretchy skin, so it cannot simply expand as the animal grows. A new, looser cuticle forms underneath the old one while the caterpillar keeps eating, and once there is no room left inside the old layer, the caterpillar splits it open and crawls out wearing the new one. That cycle repeats several times before it is finally ready to form its chrysalis.

items.prompt: How does a butterfly drink nectar through a mouth that looks like a coiled spring?

options.label: It bites off pieces of flower and chews them
options.feedback: An adult butterfly has no jaws for biting or chewing; its mouthparts form a tube, not a pair of jaws.

options.label: It uncoils a long tube called a proboscis and draws liquid up through it
options.feedback: Relaxing the coil straightens the tube so it can reach down into a flower and draw nectar upward.

options.label: It presses its whole head into the flower and soaks nectar up like a sponge
options.feedback: Nothing on a butterfly's head absorbs liquid that way. The drinking happens through the narrow coiled tube alone.

options.label: It licks nectar up with a short flat tongue
options.feedback: A butterfly has no tongue of that shape; its feeding organ is a long thin tube, not a flat licking surface.

items.ok_line: A tube that coils away when it is not needed.
items.ko_title: Look at the shape of the mouthpart
items.ko_line: The spring shape belongs to a single long tube, and the question is how that tube gets used.
items.exp_title: A drinking straw that rolls up
items.exp_text: A butterfly's mouthparts form a long thin tube, the proboscis, made of two matching halves that lock together once the adult emerges. Muscles hold it coiled beneath the head like a watch spring when it is not in use, tucked out of the way of the legs. To feed, the butterfly relaxes those muscles while raising the fluid pressure inside the tube, which straightens it out and lets it reach into a flower.

items.prompt: Why do some butterfly wings shimmer and shift color as they tilt, while others look the same color from every angle?

options.label: All wing color comes from pigment, and the shimmer is just wet wings
options.feedback: Wings that shimmer do so whether they are wet or dry. The shift comes from how the scale surface is shaped, not from moisture.

options.label: Shimmering color comes from the scales' shape scattering light, while steady color comes from pigment absorbing it
options.feedback: A pigment scale keeps its color from any angle, while a structural scale's color depends on the angle light strikes it.

options.label: Only old, worn wings shimmer
options.feedback: Wear tends to dull or flake scales rather than create the shimmer. Freshly emerged wings already show it if their scales are structural.

options.label: The shimmer comes from dust the butterfly picks up while flying
options.feedback: Dust settling on a wing would dull its color rather than make it shift with viewing angle. The shimmer is built into the scale itself.

items.ok_line: Pigment holds its color; structure bends light instead.
items.ko_line: One kind of scale absorbs light for its color, the other kind scatters it.
items.exp_title: Two ways to make a color
items.exp_text: A butterfly's wing is covered in tiny overlapping scales, and each one makes color one of two ways. Some scales hold pigment that absorbs certain wavelengths of light and reflects the rest, giving a steady color from any angle. Others carry no pigment at all; their surface is ridged with structures so fine they bend and scatter light, and which wavelength scatters back toward you depends on the angle you view it from.

items.prompt: What is one reliable way to tell a butterfly from a moth by looking at its antennae?

options.label: A butterfly's antennae end in a small club; a moth's are usually feathery or plain
options.feedback: The clubbed tip is a butterfly's antenna shape, useful for steadying flight, while a moth's antennae take broader or thread-like forms instead.

options.label: Butterflies have no antennae at all
options.feedback: Every butterfly has a pair of antennae; they are simply shaped differently from a moth's.

options.label: Moths have antennae only while they are caterpillars
options.feedback: An adult moth keeps its antennae; in fact they are often larger and more elaborate than a caterpillar's small sensory stubs.

options.label: A butterfly's antennae are always longer than its whole body
options.feedback: Butterfly antennae are usually shorter than the body, not longer. Length is not what sets the two groups apart.

items.ok_line: Check the tip, not the timing.
items.ko_title: The antenna tip is the clue
items.ko_line: One group's antennae thicken into a small knob at the end; the other's do not.
items.exp_text: A butterfly's antennae are thin stalks that thicken into a small club right at the tip, useful for steadying flight and sensing air currents. A moth's antennae instead take other forms — often broad and feathery, built to catch faint airborne scent, or simple thread-like filaments with no club. Checking the tip works better than checking when an insect flies, since a few butterflies fly at dusk and a few moths fly by day.

items.prompt: How does a male butterfly find a female of his own species over a distance?

options.label: He listens for the sound of her wings beating
options.feedback: Butterflies have no ears tuned to wingbeats. Finding a mate over distance relies on scent, not sound.

options.label: He follows a scent trail she releases, sensed through receptors on his antennae
options.feedback: Sensory hairs along his antennae detect faint traces of her scent and let him track it back to its source.

options.label: He watches for a flash of wing color visible from far away
options.feedback: Color is only useful once he is close enough to see it clearly. Over real distance it fades below what eyes can pick out.

options.label: He circles at random until he happens to land near her
options.feedback: Random circling would rarely succeed. He instead steers toward a specific chemical signal carried on the air.

items.ok_line: A signal in the air, read by the antennae.
items.ko_line: At real distance, the antennae are doing the searching, not the eyes or the ears.
items.exp_title: Following a scent through open air
items.exp_text: A female butterfly releases a chemical signal called a pheromone, built to match her own species and no other. Along a male's antennae sit many tiny sensory hairs, each tuned to detect a trace of that chemical carried on the breeze. By turning until the signal grows stronger on one side, he can trace it back to its source even when she is too far off to see, then close the distance and confirm her with sight and touch.

items.prompt: How does a female butterfly choose the right plant on which to lay her eggs?

options.label: She lays on whichever plant happens to be closest to where she emerged
options.feedback: Distance alone would often place eggs on a plant her caterpillars cannot eat. She checks the plant itself before laying.

options.label: She lands and tastes the leaf with receptors on her feet before deciding
options.feedback: Chemical receptors on her feet detect the particular compounds that mark the right host plant for her caterpillars.

options.label: She releases her eggs in flight and lets them fall onto whatever is below
options.feedback: Eggs released in flight would scatter onto bare ground and rooftops as often as leaves. She lands and lays them directly on a chosen leaf.

options.label: She copies whichever plant other females were seen choosing
options.feedback: She has no way to observe and copy another female's earlier choice. Her own tasting of the leaf decides it.

items.ok_line: A taste test with her feet, before a single egg is laid.
items.ko_line: The plant is tested chemically, not chosen by distance or by copying.
items.exp_text: A caterpillar can only eat certain plants, so the female's choice of where to lay decides whether her eggs will hatch into caterpillars that can feed at all. Chemical receptors on her feet let her taste a leaf's surface the moment she lands, checking for the compounds that mark her caterpillar's particular host plant. Only once that match is confirmed does she curl her body and lay her eggs on its underside.

items.prompt: How does a monarch butterfly complete a migration that no single monarch lives long enough to finish alone?

options.label: One long-lived monarch makes the whole round trip by itself
options.feedback: No monarch generation lives long enough to fly the full round trip on its own; the journey is divided instead.

options.label: The journey is split across several generations, each covering part of the route
options.feedback: One generation flies south and overwinters, and its short-lived offspring carry the return trip north in stages.

options.label: Monarchs are carried the whole way by wind currents without flying under their own power
options.feedback: Monarchs actively fly and steer the route themselves; wind can help or hinder, but it does not carry them the whole way.

options.label: Only the eggs make the journey, carried between regions by birds
options.feedback: Monarch eggs are laid on plants where they are found, not transported by other animals between regions.

items.ok_line: A relay, handed from one generation to the next.
items.ko_title: No single flyer does it all
items.ko_line: The distance is real, but it is covered by a sequence of generations, not one animal.
items.exp_text: Monarchs that fly south in autumn belong to a special generation, built to live for months instead of weeks so they can complete the long flight and wait out winter. In spring they fly partway back and lay eggs, and it is their short-lived offspring, then their offspring's offspring, that carry the journey the rest of the way north over summer. The monarchs that finally fly south again the next autumn head for a place none of them has ever seen.

items.prompt: Why does a newly emerged butterfly sit still with its wings small and crumpled before it can fly?

options.label: Its wings are still growing new cells over the following days
options.feedback: No new wing cells are added after emergence; the wing is already complete, only folded and unexpanded.

options.label: It is pumping fluid into the wing veins to expand them to full size
options.feedback: The pumped fluid presses each wing outward through its veins, stretching it from a crumpled pad into its full flat shape.

options.label: It is simply waiting for its wings to dry off after being wet
options.feedback: The wings are not wet from the outside; what changes them is fluid pumped from within, not moisture drying off.

options.label: Its wings are already full size but folded, and it only needs to unfold them
options.feedback: The wings genuinely grow larger during this time; they are not already full size waiting to be unfolded like a fan.

items.ok_line: The wing has to be filled out before it can be used.
items.ko_line: The change is a wing growing to its true size, driven by fluid pressure from inside the body.
items.exp_title: Wings that fill out after they open
items.exp_text: The wings of a butterfly leaving its chrysalis are soft and folded into a small space, nowhere near their final shape. Its heart pumps hemolymph, the fluid that fills an insect's body, into the network of veins running through each wing, and the pressure of that fluid pushes the wing out flat and stretches it to full size. Only once the wings have expanded and their veins have stiffened as the fluid dries within them does the butterfly risk its first flight.
